topic: Baseline measurement before building
front: Why is measuring the current manual process a prerequisite for the build rather than something you can add after launch?
back: Without a pre-build baseline — handling time, error rate, cost per case, volume, rework rate — there is nothing to compare against, so "is it working?" becomes an argument about impressions. A baseline also sometimes reveals the human process is already good enough, which kills a bad project cheaply.
hook: Stems where a sponsor declares the system a success or a failure post-launch but no pre-launch number exists: the answer establishes the baseline, retroactively if necessary.

topic: Distinguishing an LLM problem from a deterministic one
front: A finance team asks for Claude to compute regulatory capital ratios from structured ledger data. What is wrong with the request?
back: The task is deterministic arithmetic over already-structured inputs. A calculation engine gets it exactly right, auditably, at negligible cost, every time. Reserve inference for the genuinely linguistic or judgemental parts: reading unstructured filings, classifying ambiguous entries, drafting the narrative. Route the numbers to code and the language to the model.
hook: When a stem describes exact, reproducible computation over structured data, the LLM is wrong for that step even when it is right elsewhere in the same flow.

topic: Turning a vague acceptance criterion into a measurable one
front: A sponsor's acceptance criterion is "the summaries should be good." Convert that into something you could actually be held to.
back: Name the population (which documents), the instrument (a held-out eval set with a written rubric, or a human-rated sample), the threshold, the measurement cadence, and who adjudicates disagreement between raters. A criterion without an instrument and an adjudicator is not a criterion; it is a hope with a number attached.
hook: Acceptance criteria in a stem that lack a measurement instrument are the defect. The best option supplies how it is measured and by whom, not a higher threshold.

topic: Stakeholders discovered too late
front: Beyond the sponsor and the engineering team, which stakeholders most often surface too late on an enterprise Claude project?
back: The owners of the data (access, residency, retention), the approvers of the risk (security, legal, privacy, compliance, model risk), and the people who will actually use the output or be measured by it. Discovering any of these after design turns their input into rework or a launch block rather than a requirement.
hook: Stems that end with a surprise veto — "legal blocked go-live" — are testing whether approvers were mapped during discovery, not whether you can now negotiate your way out.

topic: Sequencing the first use case out of a discovery portfolio
front: Discovery surfaces twelve candidate use cases. Why is starting with the highest-business-value one usually the wrong sequencing decision?
back: The first delivery has to prove the delivery mechanism as much as the use case: data access, review workflow, eval harness, deployment path, approval route, run-team model. Choose a case with real but modest value and high feasibility so those rails get built under low stakes, then reuse them for the high-value case.
hook: Triage stems give you a value axis and a feasibility axis. The trap is optimising value alone; the first case is partly chosen to de-risk everything that follows it.

topic: Eliciting tacit expertise from a subject-matter expert
front: A claims specialist cannot articulate the rules they use to flag a suspicious claim. What do you ask for instead of rules?
back: Worked examples. Ask for a few dozen recently handled cases with the decision and one sentence of reasoning, deliberately including borderline calls and ones later reversed. Tacit expertise is recovered far more reliably from labelled instances than from an attempted rule list, and those instances become your first eval set and few-shot pool.
hook: When a stem says the expert "just knows," the answer collects cases, not rules. Recognise the second payoff: the same artefact serves discovery, evaluation, and prompting.

topic: What makes an ADR useful later
front: Why is an architecture decision record that lists only the chosen option nearly worthless six months after it was written?
back: An ADR's value is the rejected alternatives, why each lost, and the constraints in force at the time. Without them a future engineer cannot tell whether the decision still holds or whether a constraint has changed and invalidated it, so they either re-litigate from zero or preserve it superstitiously.
hook: ADR items hinge on context and rejected options, not on the decision itself. An option that says "document the decision and its rationale" but omits alternatives is incomplete.

topic: False precision when reporting eval results upward
front: Your pipeline scored 91% on a 200-case eval set. How should that figure appear in a paper going to an executive committee?
back: As an estimate with its uncertainty and its scope: approximately 91% on a 200-case sample drawn from last quarter's traffic, with an interval, and a note on which case types are under-represented. A bare 91% invites someone to copy it into a contract as a guarantee over all future traffic.
hook: Any option that carries an eval number into an external commitment without the sample, the interval, and the population it came from is the trap, however accurate the number is.

topic: Executive versus technical framing of one decision
front: The same routing-architecture decision must be presented to the CTO's staff meeting and to the platform team. What actually changes between them?
back: The decision does not change; the supporting evidence does. Executives need the business consequence, the cost and risk envelope, the options considered, and what you need from them. Engineers need the mechanism, the failure modes, the interfaces, and the operational burden they will carry. Each audience gets what answers their decision.
hook: Framing items are not about simplifying for executives. They are about which evidence answers that audience's question; options that merely "remove technical detail" are usually wrong.

topic: Calibrated risk language
front: Why does "the system may occasionally produce an incorrect summary" fail as a risk statement to a risk committee or a regulator?
back: It is uncalibrated: no frequency, no severity, no detection method, no remediation, no owner. A usable statement gives the observed rate band from evaluation, the worst realistic consequence, how the error is detected, who is accountable, and the compensating control. Unquantified hedging reads as evasion or as an implicit claim of negligibility.
hook: Risk-communication items reward frequency plus severity plus control plus owner. "Occasionally", "rarely", and "minimal" with no number behind them are the distractor pattern.

topic: TCO beyond the inference bill
front: A business case for a Claude-based system is built purely from projected token spend. Which material cost lines are missing?
back: Human review and escalation handling, evaluation set construction and re-labelling, retrieval infrastructure and index refresh, observability and log retention, prompt and model maintenance across version changes, security and compliance review, incident response, and the run team's standing time. On many systems the inference bill is not the largest line.
hook: TCO stems plant an attractively small API figure. The correct option adds the ongoing human and operational lines — especially review labour — rather than more infrastructure.

topic: Choosing the right unit for an ROI narrative
front: Why is "cost per API call" a misleading unit in a Claude system's ROI narrative, and what should replace it?
back: Cost per successfully completed business task — including retries, failed attempts, escalations to a human, and the review minutes each outcome consumes. A cheaper tier that escalates twice as often can raise the true unit cost while lowering the API line. The denominator must be the outcome the business buys.
hook: Cost-reduction stems where a cheaper tier increases escalation volume are testing exactly this substitution. Read the denominator in every option before comparing the numbers.

topic: Answering the "why not just fine-tune" challenge
front: A stakeholder asks why you are not fine-tuning a model for their document-classification task. What is the defensible answer?
back: Fine-tuning fits stable, narrow, high-volume tasks where you hold thousands of clean labels and the behaviour resists expression in a prompt. It buys you a labelling programme, a retraining loop on every taxonomy change, and model version management. Exhaust prompting, retrieval, and evaluation first; often you never reach the threshold.
hook: The fine-tuning challenge tests whether you can state the conditions that would justify it. Options that dismiss it outright, or adopt it without naming those conditions, both fail.

topic: SLA and SLO negotiation for a probabilistic system
front: Negotiating an SLA for a Claude-based triage service, what can you put in the contract and what must you refuse?
back: Commit to availability, latency percentiles, throughput, incident response and resolution times, and a measured quality target against a named eval set with a stated refresh cadence and a remediation path. Refuse per-request correctness guarantees: identical inputs are not guaranteed identical outputs, so the unit of commitment is a population, not a call.
hook: Any option promising deterministic per-request correctness from an LLM is wrong however carefully hedged. The right one moves the guarantee to an aggregate over a defined population.

topic: Setting expectations on non-determinism
front: A product owner files a bug: the same document was summarised twice and the two summaries differed. How do you respond?
back: That is expected behaviour, not a defect. Sampling makes outputs vary; you can reduce variance but not eliminate it. Redirect to whether both outputs are acceptable under the agreed rubric. If byte-identical repeat reads are genuinely required, that is an architecture requirement — persist the first result and serve the stored artefact.
hook: A reproducibility complaint in a stem tests two things: naming non-determinism as expected, and knowing that storing and re-serving the output is how you get identical repeats.

topic: Why a successful pilot is not production evidence
front: A six-week pilot with twelve friendly users reported 94% satisfaction. Why does that not establish production readiness?
back: Pilot users self-select, tolerate faults, and often supply inputs they curated. Production brings malformed and adversarial inputs, peak concurrency, the long tail of edge cases, and users with no stake in the project. Readiness requires load evidence, an eval over representative production-shaped traffic, and the operational apparatus — not enthusiasm.
hook: High pilot satisfaction is a setup. The wrong answer scales the pilot out; the right one names the specific evidence a friendly-user pilot structurally could not produce.

topic: Production readiness review artefacts specific to LLM features
front: Which artefacts should a production readiness review demand for an LLM feature that it would not demand for a conventional service?
back: The eval set with current scores and the sample they were measured on; prompt and model versions pinned in source control; guardrail configuration; the human escalation path and its staffed capacity; logging sufficient to reconstruct a past decision; a rollback plan; and quality-drift monitors with agreed alert thresholds.
hook: PRR stems list several artefacts and omit one. The omission is usually the eval set, the escalation capacity, or the ability to reproduce a decision made months ago.

topic: Runbook content for handoff to a run team
front: What must an AI system's runbook contain so a run team can act at 3am without the build team on the call?
back: Known failure modes with their symptoms; how to distinguish a model-quality problem from an infrastructure problem; the degradation and fallback switches and who may pull them; escalation contacts; how to replay a failed request; what must not be changed without the owning team; and the monitors that indicate quality rather than uptime.
hook: Handoff stems offer "comprehensive documentation" as bait. The stronger answer is specific: failure modes, decision rights, and the model-versus-infrastructure discrimination step.

topic: Diagnosing stalled adoption after a clean launch
front: Adoption of a launched Claude assistant stalls at 15% of the target team despite strong eval scores. Where do you look first?
back: At the workflow, not the model. Common causes: it lives outside the tool people already work in; trust was lost to early visible errors that were never explained; the time it saves is smaller than the review it demands; nobody was trained and there is no local champion. Quality is necessary, not sufficient.
hook: When a stem pairs strong technical metrics with weak usage, "improve the prompt" is never the answer. Look at workflow integration, trust repair, and enablement.

topic: Deprecating a prompt or model version with live consumers
front: You must retire v1 of a prompt and model configuration that three downstream teams call. What does responsible deprecation require here that plain software deprecation does not?
back: Run v1 and v2 concurrently behind versioned interfaces; publish a behavioural diff produced by scoring both versions on the same eval set, not just a changelog; set a dated sunset with a migration window; instrument v1 to see who still calls it; and archive the v1 configuration and logs for as long as its decisions must stay defensible.
hook: AI deprecation adds two requirements: a behavioural diff on a shared eval set, and retention of the retired configuration so past decisions can still be reconstructed.
